quote: Endlichkeit der höheren Combinanten: $J(f+\varphi g, g) = J(f,g)$ wo $\varphi$ beliebig ist. z. B. Resultante.
english: Finiteness of the higher combinants: $J(f+\varphi g, g) = J(f,g)$, where $\varphi$ is arbitrary. E.g. the resultant.
topic: A list of research notes: recovering the genus from the essential divisor of the discriminant, finiteness of higher combinants, Stieltjes' asymptotic evaluation of products of polynomial values, classifying bilinear substitution groups, and eliminating the Riemann surface from Hurwitz's investigations.

triage.modern_statement: Take binary forms f of degree m and g of degree n, with m ≥ n. Let a form φ of degree m−n act by (f,g) ↦ (f+φg, g). For fixed φ this map is linear, so it is a linear action of a vector (unipotent, additive) group G_a^(m−n+1). Hilbert calls the SL2-invariants (or covariants) J(f,g) that this action leaves unchanged 'higher combinants'. They depend on g and on f only modulo g. The resultant Res(f,g) is the standard example, invariant up to a power of g's leading coefficient. The question is whether the algebra of these joint invariants is finitely generated, i.e. a Gordan/Hilbert-type finiteness theorem for this ring. In modern terms this is a special case of Hilbert's 14th problem: finite generation of invariants under a non-reductive, unipotent group (combined with SL2).
triage.answered_by: No specific later answer was found. The general framework, Hilbert's 14th problem, was settled negatively in general by Nagata (1959), whose counterexample uses an action of an additive vector group. Neither result decides this particular ring either way.

evidence.claim: Hilbert's 14th problem asks whether the ring of invariants of any representation of a linear algebraic group is finitely generated. Nagata gave the first counterexample.
Hilbert conjectured that such invariant algebras are finitely generated. Some special cases were proved, and Nagata found a counterexample in 1959.

A survey of counterexamples to Hilbert's 14th problem: invariant rings of unipotent and additive-group actions need not be finitely generated, so finiteness for such groups has to be checked case by case.
Finite generation of invariants for non-reductive (e.g. unipotent) subgroups is still studied today, for example through Grosshans subgroups and finite generation ideals.

triage.why: The diary note asks for a finiteness theorem for joint invariants of two binary forms that are unchanged by f ↦ f+φg, with the resultant as the example. The search tool hit its usage limit after two queries, and no source addressing this specific ring was found. Because the action is linear and unipotent, the question falls under Hilbert's 14th problem. Nagata's counterexample shows that finite generation can fail for such groups, so no general theorem settles the case either way. Classical results on combinants or a modern computation may exist but were not found, so the status is left as possibly unexplored.
